items.prompt: Given a sorted array and a target, find the pair whose sum is closest to the target.
items.why: Sorted + pair + 'closest' (not an exact lookup) → opposite ends. If the sum is too small, the left element can't do better with anything, so move left. A hash map can only find exact matches.

items.prompt: Given an unsorted array and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
items.why: Unsorted + original indices → hash map of value → index, O(n). Sorting for two pointers would lose the indices and cost O(n log n).

items.prompt: Move all zeroes of an array to the end in place, keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements.
items.why: In place + filter while keeping order → same-direction read/write pointers. There's no window constraint, and values aren't 1..n, so it isn't cyclic sort.

items.prompt: Given a binary array and k, return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s if you may flip at most k zeros.
items.why: Longest contiguous run under a running budget (zeros in the window ≤ k) → dynamic sliding window. You track the window's contents, not just the two end elements.

items.prompt: Return the middle node of a singly linked list in a single pass.
items.why: Linked list + middle → fast & slow pointers: fast moves 2, slow moves 1. You can't start a pointer at the tail of a singly linked list and walk it back.

items.prompt: Return true if a string can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
items.why: Palindrome check → compare the ends and move inward. On the first mismatch, try skipping either side once. It's O(n), not a subsequence DP.

items.prompt: Given two lists of closed intervals, each sorted and pairwise disjoint, return their intersection.
items.why: The items are intervals and the question is about overlap → merge intervals. You walk both lists with an index each, but the deciding signal is the overlap logic (max of starts, min of ends).

items.prompt: Given an array and a target, count the triplets i < j < k with nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] < target.
items.why: Triplets + a sum comparison; the order of values doesn't matter, so sort first. Fix one element, then run opposite ends: when the sum is small enough, every right index between them also works, so count right − left at once. O(n²).
